context:
Start with a correction, because it is the most useful thing this page can offer. The two measures in this site's tracked list for Arkansas, Senate Resolution 7 and House Resolution 1013 from the 2026 fiscal session, are not artificial intelligence bills. Both are identically titled resolutions authorizing introduction of a nonappropriation bill to amend the requirements for a digital asset mining business and the authority of local governments over such businesses. Neither mentions artificial intelligence. They are keyword false positives, swept in because cryptocurrency mining and data center policy share vocabulary with AI infrastructure policy, and both died at sine die adjournment on 29 April 2026. Arkansas holds a short fiscal session in even numbered years, which limits what can be introduced, so the near empty 2026 record is expected.

The real legislative activity happened in the 2025 regular session of the 95th General Assembly, where Arkansas enacted five AI laws in a single year. Act 159 extends publicity and likeness rights to cover AI created images, voice simulations and likenesses, restricting commercial use of a person's identifiable attributes without consent. Act 827 addresses deepfake visual material of a sexual nature and creates the criminal offense of unlawful distribution of deepfake visual material. Act 977 criminalizes creating, possessing and distributing AI generated child sexual abuse material that appears indistinguishable from a real child, with carve outs for law enforcement and legitimate research. Act 848 requires public entities to adopt formal policies governing artificial intelligence and automated decision tools, with human oversight requirements, employee training and public accessibility. Act 927 settles ownership of generative AI output, providing that the person supplying the inputs owns the result unless the work is created within employment, in which case the employer owns it. Taken together this is a coherent package covering identity, sexual exploitation, government use and intellectual property, and it is broader than what most states produced in the same year.

Arkansas has no comprehensive consumer data privacy act. The general statutes that reach AI conduct are the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act at Title 4 Chapter 88 of the Arkansas Code, which prohibits deceptive and unconscionable practices in business and gives the Attorney General investigative and enforcement authority, and the state's Personal Information Protection Act, which requires reasonable security for personal information and notification when it is breached. Neither mentions artificial intelligence. Both apply to an AI vendor that overstates its product, misrepresents automated decisions, or loses control of the personal data it trained on or collected.

Attorney General Tim Griffin has been more visible on artificial intelligence than most of his peers, though visibility is not the same as enforcement. On 13 January 2026 he created a Senior Advisor for AI role and appointed Deputy General Counsel Kevin Lee to it, with a remit covering training for law enforcement and the legal community, work with agencies and academic institutions on investigative tools, and identifying emerging risks from AI misuse. In May 2026 his office ran an Emerging Issues Series event on AI in legal practice that drew more than 400 registrants. On the federal question he has been direct, joining thirty nine other attorneys general in opposing the proposed ten year federal moratorium on state AI regulation and publicly welcoming its removal from federal legislation on 1 July 2025. He has also joined a 54 attorney general coalition urging Congress to establish an expert commission on AI and child exploitation. No formal Arkansas AI enforcement action against a company has been identified.

reading.body:
Arkansas's 2026 fiscal session produced no AI legislation, and the two measures tracked as AI bills are digital asset mining resolutions that never mention artificial intelligence.

The pattern is a state whose AI lawmaking is concentrated in one year and one subject area. Five laws enacted in the 2025 regular session cover likeness rights, sexual deepfakes, AI-generated child sexual abuse material, public entity use policies, and ownership of generative output. That is a coherent package built around identity, exploitation, government procurement, and intellectual property. It is not a framework for compute, data centers, or grid load, and nothing in the record addresses them.

The 2026 fiscal session is short by design in even numbered years, which limits what can be introduced, so the near empty record is structural rather than a signal of retreat. The two resolutions that failed, SR7 and HR1013, concerned local authority over digital asset mining businesses. They are worth noting precisely because they are not AI bills: cryptocurrency mining and data center policy share vocabulary with AI infrastructure policy, and keyword tracking conflates them. A reader looking for Arkansas's posture on power and siting will not find it here.

Enforcement is the gap. The Attorney General has created a senior AI advisor role, run a training event with more than 400 registrants, and joined multistate coalitions opposing a federal moratorium on state AI regulation and urging a congressional commission on AI and child exploitation. No formal Arkansas AI enforcement action against a company has been identified. The general statutes that would reach AI conduct, the Deceptive Trade Practices Act and the Personal Information Protection Act, do not mention artificial intelligence, and Arkansas has no comprehensive consumer data privacy act. The data covers legislative text, one municipal policy, and the Attorney General's public activity. It does not cover litigation, utility proceedings, or data center siting, which is where the compute constraint would actually appear.
